name: rusqlite bulk inserts (cached prepared statements, multi-row batches, one transaction)
baseline: rusqlite inserting one row per execute call in a loop, with the same SQLite PRAGMAs
verdict_reason: Reusing a prepared statement and inserting 50 rows per statement cut 100 million inserts from about 3 minutes to 34.3 seconds. But every run also turned off SQLite's journal and fsync, which the author says not to use in production, and the data is from 2021 on a laptop.
tier_reason: Independent of the rusqlite authors, with public code and the machine stated, but no rustc version or flags.
claimed_speedup: 100M rows: naive per-row loop about 3 minutes; reused prepared statement about a minute; prepared statement with 50-row batches 34.3 seconds (about 5x vs the loop, derived from page data).
workload: Insert 100 million rows of random (area code, age, active flag) into a 4-column SQLite table, single writer, inside one transaction for the batched versions.
hardware: MacBook Pro 2019, 2.4 GHz quad-core Intel i5, 8 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD
install: cargo add rusqlite (use Connection::transaction and prepare_cached)
one_liner: Batching SQLite inserts through rusqlite's cached prepared statements cut 100M inserts from about 3 minutes to 34 seconds.
how_it_is_fast: Preparing the INSERT once with prepare_cached skips SQL parsing and planning on every row, and a 50-row VALUES list amortizes each statement step across many rows. Wrapping everything in one transaction avoids a commit per row. The PRAGMAs (journal_mode OFF, synchronous 0, large cache, exclusive locking) remove most of the remaining I/O cost.
use_it_when: Loading or generating large SQLite databases (test fixtures, imports, ETL)
Any hot insert path: prepared-statement reuse and transactions are safe and cheap wins
skip_it_when: Production databases that must survive a crash: do not copy journal_mode OFF or synchronous 0
Few, scattered writes where per-statement overhead is not the bottleneck
caveats: 2021 data on a 2019 laptop with rusqlite 0.25.3
All Rust variants ran with journaling and fsync disabled, so the absolute times overstate what a durable setup gets
An in-memory database ran only about 2 seconds faster, so disk I/O was not the bottleneck once durability was off
tradeoffs: Batched multi-row statements need careful parameter handling and a fixed batch size
One long transaction holds the write lock for its whole duration

The machine I am using is MacBook Pro, 2019 (2.4 GHz Quad Core i5, 8GB, 256GB SSD, Big Sur 11.1)
